overview.body:
**Nishinakahime** ​(*nishinakahime*) — ‌Rice, ‌Agriculture · ​Day-sun wave ​princess ​— belongs ​to ​the Japanese ‌tradition, where ​it ​is catalogued ‌under ​the domain ‌"Rice, Agriculture". ​The ‌name means ​"Day-sun ​wave princess"[^1].

​**Nishinakahime** is ​the ​Japanese goddess ‌of ​potter's clay ‌— ​the kami ‌the *Kojiki* ​writes ‌波邇夜須毘売 and ​reads ‌*Hani-yasu-hime*, 'the ​clay that ​yields.' ‌Born, with ‌her ‌brother, from ​the dying ​goddess ‌Izanami's body, ​she ​is the ‌divinity potters ​invoke ​when earth ‌must ​soften into ‌vessel: ​patroness of ​the kiln, ​the ​wheel, and ‌Japan's ‌thousand-year ceramic ​tradition.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌restores ​the name ​as ‌**Nishinakahime** and ‌serves its ‌temple ‌at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/nishinakahime/). ‌The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent form ​— ​a description ‌computed ​from the ​displayed ​form itself. ‌The plain ​ASCII ​form *nishinakahime* ​survives ‌as a ​modern convenience ‌imposed ​by the ‌early ​domain-name system; ‌the restoration, ‌not ​the fallback, ​is ​the form ​the project ‌defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Japanese ​characters as ​**日子波邇夜須毘売命**. ​Etymologically it ​means ​"Day-sun wave ‌princess"[^1].

The ​ASCII ​form *nishinakahime* ‌survives ​only because ‌the ​early domain-name ‌system could ​not ​carry diacritics; ​it ​is a ​technological ‌compromise, not ​an ancient ‌spelling. ​The Unicode ‌restoration ​**Nishinakahime** recovers ‌the full ​diacritic ‌detail of ​the ​scholarly transliteration ‌directly ‌in the ‌address bar. ​The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ‌form ​— a ​description ‌computed from ​the displayed ​form ‌itself.

The ​letter-by-letter ‌transformation runs:

- ​**n** → ​**N** ​— Same, ​capitalized
- ‌**i** → ‌**i** ​— Same
- ‌**s** → ​**s** ​— Same
- ‌**h** ‌→ **h** ‌— ‌Same
- **i** ​→ **i** ‌— ​Same
- **n** ​→ ​**n** — ‌Same

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of the ‌name is ‌**/ni.ɕi.na.ka.hi.me/** — Modern ​Standard Japanese (Hepburn).[^1]

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- **Ni-** — ​Alveolar nasal [n] ​plus close ‌front [i] — ​light and short.
- ​**-shi-** — ‌Voiceless alveolo-palatal fricative ​[ɕ] plus [i]; ‌the soft 'shee' ​of the ‌Hepburn reading.
- **-naka-** ​— Alveolar nasal ​[n], open ​central [a], voiceless ​velar [k], open ​central [a] ‌— level and ​even.
- **-hime** — ‌Glottal [h], ​[i], bilabial [m], ‌close-mid [e]; in ​the Kojiki's spelling, ‌毘売 marks ​the feminine -hime, ‌'princess'.

For the ​modern speaker, ​the closest approximation ‌is: 'NEE-shee-nah-kah-hee-meh' — ‌the Hepburn ‌reading of the ​restored form. The ​Kojiki's name, ‌波邇夜須毘売, reads 'HAH-nee-YAH-soo ​HEE-meh'.

Kindred and ​historical forms of ‌the name:

- ​**Kojiki spelling** — ​波邇夜須毘売神 (Hani-yasu-hime-no-kami) — ‌hani 埴 ​'potter's clay' + ‌yasu 安 'easy, ​workable': the ​clay that yields
- ​**Nihon Shoki spelling** ​— 埴山姫 (Haniyama-hime) ‌'Clay-Mountain Princess'; ‌also 埴安神 (Haniyasu-no-kami)
- ​**Japanese** — 埴輪 ‌haniwa — ​'clay rings', the ​Kofun-period terracottas; the ‌same hani ‌'clay' lives on ‌in their name

‌Nishinakahime is ​a plain restoration ‌by the mechanical ​rule: the ASCII ​form loses ​no distinctive feature. ‌The kami behind ​the name ​is the one ​the Kojiki writes ‌波邇夜須毘売神 and ​reads Hani-yasu-hime — ​'the clay that ​yields' — ‌born from Izanami's ​body in her ‌fatal illness; the ​lexicon's longer ‌original-script form 日子波邇夜須毘売命 ​carries the honorific ‌日子 and ‌the title 命. ​She is a ​minor but ​vividly attested kami ​of potter's clay, ‌not a ‌figure of the ​imperial cult.

original-script.body:
The ​name is ‌written ‌in ​Japanese characters ​as ​**日子波邇夜須毘売命**. This ​original ​script ‌is the ​form ​against ‌which the ​ASCII ‌fallback *nishinakahime* ​and ‌the ​PuniCodex restoration ​**Nishinakahime** ​are measured: ​the ​restoration ‌preserves its ​full ‌diacritic ​detail of ‌the ​written form, ‌so ​that ‌a reader ​typing ​the modern ‌address ‌still ‌speaks the ​ancient ​name.[^1]

‌The lexicon's ​original ​script **日子波邇夜須毘売命** ‌carries ​the ​core name ‌the ​*Kojiki* writes ‌**波邇夜須毘売神** ​and ​reads **Hani-yasu-hime**, ​'the ​clay that ‌yields,' ‌with ​the honorific ‌日子 ​and ​the title ‌命 ‌(-no-mikoto). The ‌Nihon ‌Shoki ​writes the ‌same ​goddess **埴山姫** ​(Haniyama-hime), ​'Clay-Mountain ‌Princess' — ​the ​埴 ​(hani, 'potter's ‌clay') ​element written ​directly. ​The ‌restored form ​**Nishinakahime** ‌romanizes the ​Hepburn ‌reading ​of the ‌lexicon's ‌longer ​spelling; the ​traditional ​reading of ​the ‌Kojiki ‌name is ​Hani-yasu-hime.

sources.citation: Kojiki (birth of Kagutsuchi; Hani-yasu-biko and Hani-yasu-hime).

domains.body:
**Nishinakahime** ​is the ‌Japanese goddess ‌of ​potter's clay ​— the ​kami the ​*Kojiki* ​writes 波邇夜須毘売 ‌and reads ​*Hani-yasu-hime*, ​'the clay ‌that yields.' ​Born, ‌with her ​brother, from ‌the ​dying goddess ​Izanami's body, ​she is ​the ​divinity potters ‌invoke when ​earth ‌must soften ​into vessel: ‌patroness ​of the ‌kiln, the ​wheel, ‌and Japan's ​thousand-year ceramic ​tradition.[^1]

### Potter's ‌Clay ‌(Hani)

Hani ‌埴 is ​the ​subsoil earth ‌dug for ​ceramics ​— her ‌element and ​her ​body; the ‌substance that ​takes any ‌shape ​given patience.

### ​The Yielding ​Name

​Yasu 安, ‌'easy, gentle': ‌Motoori ​Norinaga glossed ‌her name ​as ​clay kneaded ‌until it ‌softens — ‌a ‌craft instruction ​inside the ‌theology.

### ​Kagutsuchi's Fire

​Born from ​Izanami's ‌death-agony after ​the fire ​god's ​birth — ‌clay and ​flame as ​twin ​inheritances from ‌the same ​tragedy.

### ‌Kiln Ancestor ​(Tōso)

Enshrined ‌in ​Japan's pottery ‌towns from ‌Bizen ​to Seto ​as the ​kiln founders' ​patron ‌— the ‌rokkoyō's tutelary ​goddess.

sources.citation: Nihon Shoki (Haniyama-hime; Haniyasu-no-kami) — Aston, Nihongi I.

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated with ‌Nishinakahime ​concentrates ​in ​a small ​set ​of ‌recurring ​attributes, each ​a ‌compressed ​statement ‌about the ​name:[^1]

- ‌**Hani ​埴, ​potter's clay** ​— ​The ​worked ‌earth itself; ​what ‌she ​is, ‌not merely ​what ‌she ​rules.
- ‌**The kneaded ​lump** ​— ‌Clay ‌worked until ‌it ​yields ​(hani-neyasu): ‌patience made ​visible, ​the ‌potter's ​first offering.
- ​**Kiln ‌flame** ​— ‌Kagutsuchi's fire ​tamed ​by ​craft ​— the ‌second ‌element ​that ‌turns earth ​into ​vessel.
- ‌**Haniwa ‌cylinders** — ‌The ‌'clay ​rings' ‌of the ​Kofun ​tombs, ​named ‌for the ​same ​hani ​— ‌her element's ​most ​famous ​archaeological ‌form.
- **The ​unglazed ‌vessel** ​— ‌The tea-bowl ​aesthetic ‌of ‌wabi: ​value found ​precisely ​where ​the ‌clay is ‌least ​disguised.

sources.citation: Kojiki (birth of Kagutsuchi; Hani-yasu-biko and Hani-yasu-hime).

mythology.body:
Nishinakahime's mythology is two ​sentences long in the Kojiki — and they ‌are among the most striking in the whole ‌canon. Everything else the tradition knows about her ​is in her name: hani, potter's clay, and ​yasu, the yielding. The potters of Japan's ancient ​kiln towns supplied the rest of her ​story — a thousand years of practice laid ​at her feet.[^1]

### The Dying Goddess Bears the ‌Clay Kami (Kojiki)

Izanami gave birth to the ​fire god Kagutsuchi, and the fire burned her ​so badly that she sickened and lay dying. ‌From her body in its extremity came ​the last kami of the living generation: from ‌her vomit, the metal-mountain deities Kanayamahiko and Kanayamahime; ​from her urine, the water goddess Mizuha-no-me; and ‌from her bowels, the brother and sister of ​clay — Hani-yasu-biko and Hani-yasu-hime (Kojiki, birth of ​Kagutsuchi; the Nihon Shoki gives her the ​parallel names Haniyama-hime, 'Clay-Mountain Princess,' and Haniyasu-no-kami). The ​texts state this with the same flat calm ​as everything else in the divine genealogies, yet ‌the implication is immense: the kami of humanity's ​three great materials — metal, water, clay ‌— are born from the mother's death-agony. In ​Shinto's most radical birth story, the technologies that ‌make civilization possible are not stolen from heaven ​or won by conquest; they are what a ‌dying goddess leaves behind.[^2]

### A Name That Means ​'Clay That Yields' (Name)

Hani-yasu is a ‌name that explains itself, the way kami names ​so often do. *Hani* (埴) is potter's clay, ​the earth dug from the subsoil that holds ‌water and takes any shape; *yasu* (安/易) is ‌'easy, gentle, workable.' The goddess is, literally, the ‌clay that yields — earth soft enough ​to form. The great Kokugaku scholar Motoori Norinaga, ​in his *Kojikiden*, glossed the name as *hani-neyasu*: ‌clay kneaded and worked until its stiffness softens ​and it becomes obedient to the hand. The ​spelling is itself a lesson: the Kojiki's characters ‌波邇夜須 are phonetic choices made for sound ​rather than sense, which is why later writers ​preferred the semantic form 埴, 'clay,' that the ‌Nihon Shoki uses in Clay-Mountain Princess. Shinto rarely ​makes abstract theology; here the theology is a ‌craft instruction. The name is a recipe: work ​the clay until it yields — and ​to read the name correctly is already to ​know what she is.

### Three Gifts of Civilization ​from One Body (Kojiki)

Read together, the kami ‌born from Izanami's failing body form a complete ‌inventory of material culture. Kanayama-hime, from the vomit, ​is metal — ore, smelting, the smith's ‌art. Mizuha-no-me, from the urine, is water — ​wells, irrigation, the pure stream. And Hani-yasu-hime, from ​the feces, is clay — the kiln, the ‌pot, the fired vessel that outlives its maker. ‌Japan confirmed the inventory in its shrines: the ‌clay siblings are enshrined in pottery districts ‌as the kiln ancestors (*tōso*), and the Kanayama ​kami at mines and smithies. The distribution of ‌a goddess's dying body across human technology is ​unique in the Kojiki: no other birth narrative ​so completely fuses physiology and craft. Her mythology ​is her etymology writ large — from ‌the body of the mother earth-goddess comes the ​very substance that, worked by human hands, holds ​grain, sake, and the ashes of the dead.

### ​The Kiln Ancestors (Folk Tradition)

The imperial chronicles ‌give Hani-yasu-hime two clauses; Japanese potters gave ​her a thousand years. The great ceramic towns ​— Bizen, Shigaraki, Echizen, Seto, Tanba, Tokoname, the ​six ancient kilns (*rokkoyō*) — enshrine the clay ‌kami as patrons and founders of their craft, ​under the titles Clay-Mountain Princess and Clay-Mountain Prince, ‌and kiln observances still open with offerings ​to the earth the pots are made from. ‌The tradition's material memory runs deeper than the ​shrines: the *haniwa*, the 'clay rings' and hollow ‌figures set on the great tombs of the ‌Kofun age (3rd–6th centuries), carry her element *hani* ​in their very name — clay that ​was never forgotten as sacred stuff. A goddess ​born in a moment of utmost indignity became ​the quiet patron of Japan's most refined art: ‌the tea bowl's wabi, the Bizen jar's unglazed ‌fire-marks — all of it earth-plus-fire, her two ​inheritances in one vessel.

syncretism.body:
Hani-yasu-hime ​was never ‌absorbed into ‌a Buddhist ​bodhisattva or ​a combinatory ​shrine the ​way Inari ​or Hachiman ‌were; the ​folk tradition ​kept her ‌discrete — ​a local ‌craft deity ​of kiln ‌and clay-pit ​— and ​her syncretism ​is better ​described as ​occupational than ‌theological. The ​meaningful comparisons ‌are pan-Eurasian. ​Across the ‌world, creator ​gods make ‌humankind from ​clay: Enki ‌and Ninhursag ​shape the ​first worker ‌from earth's ‌mud in ‌Sumerian myth; ​the K'iche' ​gods form ‌people from ​maize dough ​in the ‌*Popol Vuh*; ​Prometheus fashions ​mankind from ‌earth ​and water; ‌and in ​Hebrew tradition ​*ʾādām* is ​the one ​made from ‌*ʾădāmāh*, red ‌arable earth ​— a ‌kinship the ​Greek *adamas* ​echoes elsewhere ‌in this ‌very lexicon. ‌The Japanese ‌case is ​distinctive in ‌one detail: ​elsewhere the ​potter-god shapes ​humanity; here ‌the goddess ​is the ​clay itself, ​and what ‌is shaped ​from her ​— vessel, ​figurine, kiln-fired ‌haniwa — ​is her ‌continuing body.[^1]

​Kindred figures ‌in the ​PuniCodex cross-tradition ‌index include ‌[[anahita|Anāhitā]], [[audhumla|Auðhumla]], ​[[babaluaye|Ọbalúayé]], [[bastet|Bꜣstt]], ​[[cernunnos|Cernunnos]], and ​[[coatlicue|Cōātlīcue]], each ​linked through ‌earth / ‌mother / ​fertility.

cultural-legacy.body: Her ​legacy is ‌written into ‌the Japanese ​language and ​landscape. The ​word *hani* ​never left ​the language: ‌*haniwa*, the ​terracotta rings ​and figures ‌of the ​Kofun-period tombs, ‌are her ​name's most ‌famous compound, ​and the ​Kofun age ​(c. 250–538 ​CE) left ​them in ‌their tens ​of thousands ‌— the ​Saitobaru kofun ‌cluster in ​Miyazaki alone ‌preserves over ​three ‌hundred. The ​six ancient ​kilns (*rokkoyō*) ‌— Bizen, ‌Echizen, Seto, ‌Shigaraki, Tanba, ​Tokoname — ​still work ‌the clays ​their regions ​have yielded ‌for a ​millennium and ​a half, ‌and potters' ​guilds and ‌kiln shrines ​still honor ​the clay ​kami at ​the start ‌of the ‌firing season. ​The tea ‌ceremony, which ​elevated the ​humble, unglazed, ‌slightly irregular ‌bowl into ‌the ‌summit of ​taste, is ‌in a ​sense her ​aesthetic theology: ​value discovered ‌precisely where ​the material ​is least ​disguised. She ‌has no ​festival on ​the national ​calendar and ‌no seat ​in the ‌imperial rites ​— her ‌cult belongs ​to the ‌workshops — ‌but anyone ​who has ​held a ​Japanese tea ​bowl has ‌held something ‌her name ​explains.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki (birth of Kagutsuchi; Hani-yasu-biko and Hani-yasu-hime).

archaeology.body: No ​shrine can ‌be ‌proven ​hers from ​inscriptions ​of ​her mythic ​era ‌— her ​attestation ​is ‌textual — ​but ‌her ​element dominates ‌the ​Japanese archaeological ​record. ​The ​*haniwa* cylinders, ​houses, ‌warriors, ​and dancing ‌figures ​of the ‌Kofun ​period ‌(3rd–6th c. ​CE) ‌are ​her name's ​material ‌echo; major ‌concentrations ‌survive ​at the ​Saitobaru ‌kofun ​group, Miyazaki ​Prefecture ‌(a designated ​Special ​Historic ‌Site), and ​the ‌Shibayama ​district of ​Chiba. ​The Sue-ware ​tradition ‌(5th–6th ‌c.) left ​hundreds ‌of ​*anagama* tunnel-kiln ​sites ‌across western ‌Japan ‌— ‌among them ​the ‌Sanage ​kiln complex ​in ​Aichi Prefecture ‌— ​whose ​grey stoneware ​marks ‌the ​arrival of ​high-fired ​ceramics. The ‌textual ​witnesses ‌are the ​Kojiki ‌(712 ​CE) and ‌the ‌Nihon Shoki ​(720 ​CE), ​both preserved ​through ‌the ‌medieval manuscript ​tradition.[^1]

meditation.body:
Shinto's honesty ​about where ‌gods come ‌from has ​no sharper ​example. The ​clay goddess ​is born ​from the ‌dying Izanami's ​excrement — ​the lowest ‌moment of ​the greatest ‌mother in ​the canon — ‌and the ​Kojiki records ​it without ​apology, in ​the same ​breath as ‌the fire ​that killed ‌her. The ​tradition refuses ‌the instinct ​to clean ‌its gods ​up. Precisely because ‌she comes ​from what ​every culture ‌is taught ‌to be ‌ashamed of, ​Hani-yasu-hime is ​the patron ‌of the ​material every ​culture actually ‌lives by: ​the worked ​earth beneath ‌the refinement, the ​clay beneath ‌the glaze.

​Her theology ​is a ​discipline of ​attention. The ‌potter at ‌the wheel ​repeats the ‌name's own ​gloss — ​knead, work, ‌wait for ‌the yielding ‌— and in ‌the yielding ​discovers that ‌matter itself ​is not ​dead but ​responsive, almost ‌willing. In ​an age ​of plastics ​and pixels, ‌clay that ​must be ​dug, kneaded, ​thrown, and fired ‌remains one ​of the ‌last materials ​that answer ‌the hand ​directly. That ‌responsiveness is ‌what her ​name means, ​and it ​is what ​the dying ‌goddess left ‌behind for ​the living.[^1]

kojiki-nihonshoki.body:
Japan's two earliest chronicles, the Kojiki (712 CE) and Nihon Shoki (720 CE), record Nishinakahime in mythic narratives of cosmogony and imperial descent. The name appears in kanji logographs whose readings were later fixed by tradition.

The restoration Nishinakahime preserves the romanized scholarly form derived from those classical sources.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki (birth of Kagutsuchi; Hani-yasu-biko and Hani-yasu-hime).

shinto-sources.body:
Shinto ritual texts, shrine records, and norito prayers preserve the cultic identity of Nishinakahime. The kami is honored at shrines associated with rice, and festival calendars perpetuate the name.

The Unicode form Nishinakahime gives that ongoing tradition a precise digital address.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki (birth of Kagutsuchi; Hani-yasu-biko and Hani-yasu-hime).

buddhist-japanese.body:
Japanese Buddhist literature and art sometimes assimilate Nishinakahime into Buddhist cosmology, mapping kami onto dharmic protectors and bodhisattvas. The honji-suijaku discourse provides a framework for such identifications.

The restored name Nishinakahime appears in both Shinto and Buddhist contexts in the PuniCodex archive.[^1]
